prompt: Somebody deletes the shop's bucket by hand, and Config Connector manages it. What happens?

choices.text: Nothing until somebody runs kubectl apply again
choices.why: That is Terraform's behaviour; the controller acts on its own.

choices.text: The controller creates it again
choices.why: Right. The object still says it should exist.

choices.text: The object in the cluster is deleted to match the bucket
choices.why: The object is the desired state; reality is made to match it, not the reverse.

choices.text: A plan is written for a person to approve
choices.why: Config Connector has no plan step.

prompt: Why is RBAC on a Config Connector namespace effectively Google Cloud IAM?
hint: Who creates the resource, with which permissions?

choices.text: Kubernetes copies its roles into IAM
choices.why: Nothing is copied; the effect comes from the controller's account.

choices.text: Google reads RBAC to decide every API call
choices.why: Google decides by the controller's service account, not by RBAC.

choices.text: Objects there act with the controller's account
choices.why: Right. Creating an object is creating a resource with its permissions.

choices.text: Namespaces and projects are the same object
choices.why: They are different things in different systems.

prompt: A namespace full of Config Connector objects is deleted by mistake. What decides whether the buckets survive?

choices.text: Whether each object carried the abandon deletion policy
choices.why: Right. Without it, deleting the object deletes the resource.

choices.text: Whether the buckets had versioning
choices.why: Versioning keeps object versions, not the bucket itself.

choices.text: Nothing: Google refuses to delete a bucket that has objects
choices.why: The controller deletes what it owns, contents and all.

choices.text: Whether a Terraform state still lists them
choices.why: Terraform plays no part in what the controller deletes.

prompt: What does Infrastructure Manager take off the team's hands, compared with running Terraform in their own pipeline?

choices.text: Writing the configuration
choices.why: The configuration is the same HCL, written by the team.

choices.text: Keeping, locking and versioning the state
choices.why: Right. Google keeps the state per deployment.

choices.text: Correcting changes made by hand between applies
choices.why: It does not correct drift; Config Connector does.

choices.text: Reading the plan
choices.why: The preview still has to be read by a person.

prompt: Whose identity does an Infrastructure Manager deployment act with when it applies?

choices.text: The identity of whoever ran the last gcloud command
choices.why: That person started it; the deployment acts as its own account.

choices.text: The project's default compute account
choices.why: The deployment names a service account of its own.

choices.text: The service account named on the deployment
choices.why: Right. Lesson 5's impersonation, made permanent.

choices.text: Google's own infrastructure account, with every permission
choices.why: No deployment gets unlimited permissions; it gets its account's.

prompt: A configuration that destroys a bucket by mistake is applied through Infrastructure Manager instead of a laptop. What is different?
hint: Does the runner change what Terraform does?

choices.text: Infrastructure Manager refuses destructive plans
choices.why: It applies what Terraform plans, destruction included.

choices.text: The bucket is moved to a recycle bin for 30 days
choices.why: There is no such bin for buckets in this flow.

choices.text: The bucket is still destroyed; the revision records it
choices.why: Right. The record is better; the outcome is the same.

choices.text: The destroy waits for Google support to approve it
choices.why: Nobody at Google reviews your plans.

prompt: Match each tool to what happens to a change made by hand.

pairs.right: it stays until the next revision
it stays until the next plan shows it

right_distractors: it is copied into the state

prompt: A team runs AWS and Google Cloud, and wants one tool and one review flow. Which fits?
hint: Which of the three speaks more than one cloud?

choices.text: Config Connector
choices.why: Google only.

choices.text: Infrastructure Manager
choices.why: It runs Terraform, but only for Google Cloud.

choices.text: Terraform, run by their own pipeline
choices.why: Right. One tool, providers for both.

choices.text: Both platform tools, one per cloud
choices.why: That is two tools, which is what they wanted to avoid.

prompt: A bucket is declared in both Terraform and Config Connector. What does each apply look like?

choices.text: The second tool refuses: the bucket has an owner
choices.why: Neither checks for another owner.

choices.text: Like it worked, while each undoes the other
choices.why: Right. Pick one owner per resource.

choices.text: They merge their settings into one bucket
choices.why: Nothing merges; each writes its own.

choices.text: Google creates a second bucket with a suffix
choices.why: Names are unique; nothing invents a suffix.

prompt: Why does the shop not use Config Connector?

choices.text: It cannot describe Cloud Storage buckets
choices.why: It can; the lesson's first file is one.

choices.text: It costs more per bucket than Terraform
choices.why: There is no per-bucket price; the cluster is the cost.

choices.text: It has no cluster to run it in
choices.why: Right. A cluster just to hold descriptions is not worth it.

choices.text: It does not support versioning on buckets
choices.why: The example enables versioning.

prompt: Put the move of a bucket from Terraform to Config Connector in a safe order.
items: Write the StorageBucket object with the same settings
Remove the resource block from the Terraform files
kubectl apply the object so the controller adopts it
trap: Applying the object before state rm is the slip: for a while the bucket has two owners.

prompt: Which of these does Config Connector have that Terraform run by a pipeline does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of drift and of state.

choices.text: Correcting drift on its own
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A plan before every change
choices.why: No. That is Terraform's, not Config Connector's.

choices.text: No state file to protect
choices.why: Yes. The objects are the desired state.

choices.text: Providers for other clouds
choices.why: No. It is Google only.

prompt: How many ways of describing the shop's bucket does the comparison table set side by side?
hint: Count the columns after the first.
